passage:
Baljeet,
I owe you an honest letter, not another post.
In March, when you asked HR for a ramp at the side entrance, I wrote that long post about standing with my colleague and tagged the whole office. It got two hundred likes. I felt great. Then you asked me to come to the facilities meeting and speak, and I said I had a client call. I didn't. Then you asked me to sign the letter to the landlord, and I said I'd look at it. I never did.
When you told me last week, "You liked being seen helping more than helping," I was angry for a day. Then I reread my post, and it was mostly about me.
So: the meeting is Thursday. I'll be there, I'll sign, and if I get something wrong, tell me. I'll listen this time.
Lokesh

qa.q: How many likes did Lokesh's post get?
qa.a: It got two hundred likes.

qa.q: Why was Lokesh angry for a day after Baljeet's comment?
qa.a: The words stung because they were true; Lokesh felt exposed, and only on rereading the post saw it was mostly about Lokesh.

qa.q: Which choices in the letter show Lokesh moving from being seen to actually helping?
qa.a: Lokesh commits to attending Thursday's meeting, signing the letter, and asking to be corrected, all of which cost more than a post.

qa.q: What would Baljeet need to see on Thursday for the letter to mean something?
qa.a: Baljeet would need Lokesh actually present and signing, since earlier promises faded as soon as effort was needed.

grounding: A young professional who posted support for a colleague's cause but dropped it when it took effort admits this and commits to listening.

subtopic: Allyship and how to help a targeted person
passage: You asked, Jasleen, so I'll be honest, even though it isn't flattering. Last year I got very loud about fair pay for the domestic workers in our housing society. Stories, a poster, a hashtag. I'm Alka, the girl with the "ally" sticker on her laptop. Then the residents' committee proposed an actual raise, and I realised it meant paying Sarojini-didi, who cooks for us, more every month. Suddenly I was busy on the meeting day. When Sarojini-didi asked if I'd speak for the workers, I said, "Let's see." She just looked at me. That look did something. I went to the next meeting, sat at the back, and mostly listened to the workers talk. One of them corrected me in front of everyone: I'd been calling it charity. It isn't. It's wages. I said, "You're right." That felt worse than the stickers, and much more real.

qa.q: What did Alka have on her laptop?
qa.a: An "ally" sticker.

qa.q: Why did Sarojini-didi's look affect Alka so much?
qa.a: It made Alka see that her loud support vanished once it cost her money, and she felt ashamed.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Alka's behaviour, and what did she change?
qa.a: After the look, she went to the next meeting, listened to the workers, and accepted a correction about charity versus wages.

qa.q: How might the workers see Alka at that second meeting?
qa.a: They might be cautious at first, remembering "Let's see", but someone who listens and says "You're right" is easier to trust than someone with stickers.

grounding: A young woman admits that her public support for workers' pay faded when it cost her, and describes learning to listen and accept correction.

subtopic: Allyship and how to help a targeted person
passage: I'm Pooja, and I've watched Irfan since he joined our office's safety committee in January. At the town hall he took the mic and said, "As a man, I want to be an ally," and the room clapped. He posted a photo with the committee banner that same evening. Then came the actual work: checking late-night cab routes, three nights a month, till eleven. Irfan came once. When Shabnam from HR pointed out that his draft rule, "women should leave by eight", put the burden on women, he said, "I was only trying to help," and stopped replying in the group. I can't know what's going on inside him. Maybe he's busy. But the banner photo is still his profile picture, and the cab checks are down to three of us.

qa.q: What did Irfan say at the town hall?
qa.a: "As a man, I want to be an ally."

qa.q: What might Irfan have felt when Shabnam pointed out the problem with his draft rule?
qa.a: He may have felt embarrassed or criticised, which could be why he said "I was only trying to help" and went quiet.

qa.q: At the moment Shabnam corrected him, what choice could Irfan have made instead?
qa.a: He could have thanked Shabnam, asked how to rewrite the rule, and kept coming to the cab checks, staying through the discomfort.

qa.q: How are Pooja and the others affected by Irfan fading out?
qa.a: They're left doing the late-night checks with fewer hands, while his banner photo still earns him credit.

grounding: A colleague watches a young man announce allyship publicly, then drift away when the work gets hard and he is corrected.

passage:
Week one. When Leela explained at the all-hands that the company website was almost impossible to use with a screen reader, Ayesha was the first to type in the team channel: "Accessibility is non-negotiable! Proud to stand with Leela ❤️" Forty reactions. She felt warm all afternoon.
Week three. The audit came back. Ayesha's own product pages had two hundred images with no descriptions. Fixing them meant her weekend. She told Leela she was "swamped", muted the accessibility thread, and changed the subject whenever it came up at lunch.
Week five. Leela stopped by her desk. "You were the loudest in week one. I haven't heard from you since the actual work started." Ayesha felt her face burn and nearly said, "I've been busy." Instead she said, "You're right. Which pages first?" Leela pulled up a chair and let her hear how the screen reader stumbled over each blank image.

qa.q: How many images on Ayesha's pages had no descriptions?
qa.a: Two hundred images.

qa.q: What was Ayesha feeling after the first post, and what does it suggest about the motive?
qa.a: She felt warm all afternoon over the forty reactions, which suggests the support was partly about being seen as good.

qa.q: What choice at Leela's desk marked Ayesha's turning point?
qa.a: Instead of saying "I've been busy", Ayesha admitted Leela was right and asked which pages to fix first, accepting the correction and staying with the uncomfortable work.

qa.q: What might the silence between week one and week five have been like for Leela?
qa.a: Leela watched loud cheering turn into a muted thread the moment effort was needed, which likely felt like being a talking point rather than being supported.

grounding: A young professional loudly backs a colleague's accessibility request for applause, drops it when it costs her weekend, then accepts correction and starts the work.

subtopic: Allyship and how to help a targeted person
passage: Kiran, before you post that, sit with your old aunt a minute. When I was twenty-five I worked in the accounts office of a cotton mill. The women spinners wanted a crèche; their babies slept on sacks beside the looms. I made a speech at the gate. A reporter took my photo, and my mother cut it out and framed it. I was very pleased with Ankita the brave. Then the manager hinted my promotion might "take longer". And the spinners asked me to come on Sundays to help list the children's names. Suddenly I was always busy. One day Kamala-bai stopped me in the yard. "You spoke for us once," she said. "Come and listen once." It stung for a week. Then I went. I sat on the floor and wrote names for three Sundays. The crèche opened the next year. The photo? I took it down. I kept the list.

qa.q: Where did the spinners' babies sleep?
qa.a: On sacks beside the looms.

qa.q: What does "I was very pleased with Ankita the brave" reveal about Ankita's early motive?
qa.a: It shows Ankita cared a lot about looking brave, the photo and the praise, more than about the crèche itself.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Ankita's story, and what choice followed?
qa.a: Kamala-bai's words, "Come and listen once", stung, and after a week Ankita chose to go and spent three Sundays on the floor writing the children's names.

qa.q: How might Kamala-bai have seen Ankita before and after those Sundays?
qa.a: At first Kamala-bai likely saw someone who used the spinners' cause for a photo and then vanished; afterwards, someone who finally listened and did the dull work.

grounding: An elder recalls backing a cause mainly for praise, backing away when it cost something, then accepting a worker's correction and staying through the hard part.
